title: App Signing, Upload Keys, CI, and Recovery

scout.purpose: Protect a real Android boundary through app signing, upload keys, ci, and recovery, rather than adding a security API without a threat.
scout.realWorldUse: Production Android security spans an attacker-controlled client, system IPC, local data, networks, backend authority, build infrastructure, and incident recovery.
scout.outcome: Model the attack, choose a proportionate control, verify its limitations, and operate its failure and recovery paths.

blocks.text: Android accepts an update when its signing identity is compatible with the installed app. With Play App Signing, Google protects the app-signing key and signs delivered APKs; the developer signs an app bundle with a separate upload key. Losing or compromising an upload key can be recovered through an upload-key reset without changing the delivered signing identity. Losing a self-managed app-signing key can prevent updates, while compromise can let an attacker impersonate the publisher. These keys require different access and incident plans.

blocks.text: Keep private keys outside repositories, developer chat, build artifacts, and ordinary CI logs. Prefer a protected signing service or tightly controlled CI secret with least privilege, approvals, audit logs, environment separation, short-lived workload identity where supported, and no forked pull-request access. Verify the artifact digest, variant, version, source revision, dependencies, and signing certificate before upload. Preserve public certificates and fingerprints for API registration; they are identifiers and can be shared.

blocks.code:
./gradlew :app:bundleRelease
apksigner verify --print-certs app-release.apk
# Compare digest and certificate with approved release metadata before upload.
blocks.caption: A focused fragment expressing the security boundary; production work must include the surrounding lifecycle and server policy.

blocks.text: Document generation, custody, backup, recovery, rotation/upgrade, revocation, staff departure, compromise, and disaster rehearsal. Play signing-key upgrades have platform-version compatibility behaviour, so plan certificate lineage and providers that pin the signing fingerprint. Test upload-key reset and emergency release authority before an incident. An attacker with CI signing access may alter source or artifact even without exporting a key, so protect the complete build-to-release path and retain provenance.

Security controls must preserve the user promise under attack, failure, recovery, and change. Record the protected asset, attacker capability, trust boundary, preconditions, prevention, detection, response, recovery, owner, and residual risk. Prefer secure platform defaults and reviewed protocols over custom cryptography or hidden client logic. Validate the exact release artifact and authoritative server boundary, then deliberately attempt bypass, replay, substitution, downgrade, stale state, account switching, process death, key loss, and partial rollout. Collect privacy-safe diagnostic evidence that distinguishes policy denial, implementation defect, dependency outage, device limitation, and active abuse. A control is production-ready only when rotation, revocation, migration, monitoring, accessibility, support, and incident response are owned and rehearsed.

blocks.title: Security theatre to avoid
blocks.text: Watch carefully for this common failure mode in production: Using the irreplaceable app-signing key directly on every developer laptop increases exposure when a separate resettable upload key could be used.

trap_check.mistake: Using the irreplaceable app-signing key directly on every developer laptop increases exposure when a separate resettable upload key could be used.
trap_check.why: The implementation either trusts the wrong boundary or ignores a lifecycle path, producing false confidence or an availability failure.
trap_check.fix: Return to the threat model, enforce authority at the correct boundary, and add evidence for bypass, change, and recovery.

trap_check.mistake: Treating an obfuscated or integrity-checked client decision as server authority.
trap_check.why: Installed clients remain observable and modifiable, and local signals can be bypassed or relayed.
trap_check.fix: Keep authoritative decisions, revocation, limits, and audit on a trusted server while using client controls as bounded layers.

challenge_intro.task: Create a signing architecture and incident runbook covering Play App Signing, upload key, CI identities, approvals, provenance, backup, reset, upgrade, and API fingerprints.
challenge_intro.successLooksLike: The deliverable names threats and assumptions, implements the narrow control, demonstrates an intended attack failing, and documents ownership, monitoring, recovery, and residual risk.

recall.prompt: Why separate the upload key from the app-signing key?
recall.answer: The upload key can authenticate releases with less exposure and can be reset without changing the delivered app-signing identity.

recall.prompt: What should happen before choosing a security API?
recall.answer: Identify the asset, attacker capability, trust boundary, abuse path, impact, and authority owner.

recall.prompt: Why must recovery be part of a security design?
recall.answer: Keys, credentials, certificates, devices, dependencies, and policies change or fail; unsafe or unavailable recovery can defeat the control and user promise.
